Composite phase change material filling structure design based on parameter analysis and thermal resistance guidance
abstract: ​Solid-liquid phase change technology plays a key role in thermal energy storage (TES). To clarify its transfer mechanisms, a coupled conduction-advection-phase-change thermal resistance framework is proposed to describe the entire phase-change process. Three parameters, the phase-change resistance (Rpc,xi), phase-change advection thermal resistance (Rpc-adv,xi), and composite phase-change convection thermal resistance (Rpc-conv,xi), are defined to quantify the role of latent-heat transport in local and overall heat transfer. Corresponding evaluation factors (Fpc,xi, Fpc, ΔFxi, ΔF) describe the spatiotemporal evolution and anisotropy of the thermal resistance field. The effects of thermophysical parameters were systematically investigated, and sensitivity analyses were performed. The results indicate that thermal conductivity (λ), specific heat capacity (cp), latent heat (La), and dynamic viscosity (μ) respectively dominate different aspects of heat-storage performance. Comprehensive optimization can effectively enhance the thermal energy storage efficiency and dynamic response of composite phase change materials (CPCMs). To integrate material design with thermal optimization, paraffin/expanded graphite CPCMs were studied under equal PW/EG ratios. Direct filling (PW–EG2 / PW–EG3) and embedded framework (PW–EG1&4-2 / PW–EG1&4-3) structures were compared. The embedded framework exhibited 80.4% and 85.8% higher total heat-storage (Q) and 19.0% and 70.1% higher average heat-storage rate ( ), with smoother interfaces, uniform thermal resistance, and stronger coupling. These findings demonstrate that coordinated regulation of material properties and structural design can significantly improve the overall performance of CPCMs, thereby enhancing the heat-storage performance of the entire TES system. This study provides valuable insights and design guidelines for the development of next-generation high-efficiency TES systems.

title: Multi-facility analysis using metered power data to quantify MRI energy use and utility bill costs across scanner operating modes
abstract: This study quantifies the energy consumption of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scanners across discrete operating modes during routine clinical workflows, based solely on electrical power measurements. Although previous studies have investigated MRI energy consumption within single hospitals or specific clinical settings, this research provides a broader and more systematic analysis. Researchers analyzed electrical power data and applied a previously developed semi-automatic method for identifying MRI operating modes using load duration curves for 20 MRI scanners across four different U.S. healthcare facilities, encompassing outpatient, inpatient, and mixed-use clinical settings. A key innovation is the inclusion of localized hourly utility rates to estimate costs, a parameter absent in prior literature. Key findings indicate significant variability in energy and cost profiles between weekdays and weekends. Scanner characteristics, including magnet strength, manufacturer, vintage, location, and clinical setting, influenced average daily energy consumption and power thresholds for operating modes. Notably, the clinical setting of a scanner predominantly determines its energy use. For example, the scanners in outpatient facilities consumed more energy. The breakdown of energy usage and costs by operating modes showed scanners spend between 61% and 93% of their time in nonproductive modes, with one outlier spending 34%. Average daily energy use for the scanners in the study ranged from 160 to 1069 kWh, with energy costs ranging from $9 to $149. This study uses an existing framework to quantify MRI energy behavior, leading to insights that can enable improved performance and cost savings across different healthcare environments.

title: Designing financial instruments for accelerated coal plant retirements: the case of China-backed coal plants in South and Southeast Asia
Improving the energy efficiency of regional integrated energy system containing hydrogen energy: a novel green energy flow-driven multi-dimensional cross-spatiotemporal decision framework
Technical, economic, and load-following capabilities assessment of grid-connected geothermal and geothermal-solar hybrid systems
abstract: The technical and economic performance as well as the load-following capabilities of grid-connected geothermal hybrid systems were assessed in this work. The analyzed geothermal hybrid configuration is composed of a binary geothermal plant integrated with a concentrating solar-thermal system and underground thermal energy storage (UTES) through a primary heat exchanger. Physics-based models for the hybrid system for plant generation capacities of 1, 25, and 50 MW were developed from validated models for each subsystem. Also, an economic model was developed that accounts for different hybrid system capabilities, solar field sizes, and thermal storage duration. The advantage of the geothermal hybrid system was assessed by comparing the performance with the baseline benchmark geothermal plant with a similar configuration and generation capacity. It was found that hybridizing geothermal plants with concentrating solar and thermal energy storage not only improves the thermal efficiency by up to 8 percentage points when additional heat from the solar-UTES loop rises the evaporator temperatures from 70 to 125 °C, but also enhances the load-following capability for the geothermal plant, which can meet a typical residential load profile with a power rate of change 0.25 kW/s with an absolute error under 13 kW for a 1 MW plant. Other benefits of hybridization include resource preservation and a potential LCOE reduction of up to 56% for a 50 MW geothermal hybrid plant having a 50% solar share, a 1.4 solar multiple, and 24-h storage capacity. The results presented in this work demonstrate that hybridizing geothermal systems transforms them into a flexible and cost-effective solution for addressing the dynamic requirements of modern electric grids.

title: A data-driven stochastic dynamic retail electricity pricing of an industrial consumer considering demand response uncertainty
Graphic criteria for hosting capability assessment of PV-EV-ESS in distribution networks
Energy flexibility estimation and forecasting in large buildings for local flexibility markets applications
abstract: Demand-side flexibility from buildings is becoming increasingly important in Nordic local flexibility markets (LFMs), where credible participation depends on accurate estimation of both the counterfactual baseline load and the flexibility that can actually be delivered. This study investigates indoor thermal modulation as a flexibility resource in four large public heat-dominated buildings in Ålesund, Norway, representing three building types and three common electric heating systems in the Nordic context. First, the flexibility potential and economic value of one-hour heating setpoint relaxations are quantified through physics-based simulation and annual Monte Carlo market analysis. Second, six forecasting approaches are compared for predicting baseline and flexible electrical loads. To address the limitations of conventional single-mode forecasters, an end-to-end pipeline, Interpretable Machine Learning for Energy Management Systems (IML-EMS), is proposed. The framework combines a differentiable gradient-boosted model with physics-informed ARX regularization derived from an RC thermal representation. Results show that directly heated buildings provide the highest flexibility, reaching 11.73 Wh/m 2 , with average LFM benefits of 0.108 NOK/m 2 . Although several benchmark models achieve competitive load-forecasting accuracy, IML-EMS provides the most reliable joint prediction of baseline and flexible load and achieves the highest bidding precision (BP) across all pilots. In addition, the model identifies interpretable RC parameters and generalizes successfully to real smart meter data, where it significantly outperforms benchmark methods.

title: A stage-adaptive optimization framework for reconciling energy balance and flexibility balance in the energy transition
Do generation diversity and renewables mitigate price shocks? Empirical evidence from the 2022 European energy crisis
abstract: Generation diversity, renewable energy supply, and self-sufficiency are commonly cited hedges against supplyrisks and price volatility in electricity markets, yet empirical validation of their effectiveness remains limited.The 2022 European energy crisis exposed electricity markets to severe price shocks driven by curtailed Russiangas imports. We use this natural experiment to test whether these factors mitigated the price shocks across38 European bidding zones. Using robust linear regression models, we relate pre-crisis system characteristics(generation diversity, renewable integration, and self-sufficiency in electricity supply) to changes in averageprices, extreme prices, and price variability. We find no evidence that greater generation diversity or self-sufficiency moderated price shocks, challenging assumptions on their protective value. Larger reservoir hydroshares are the sole predictor of lower price increases. Variable renewable energy shares do not systematicallylower either average or extreme price changes, but are associated with larger increases in day-to-day pricevariability. Natural gas shares show no robust association with price outcomes. The results suggest thatunder market coupling and marginal pricing, crisis-driven shocks transmit across bidding zones, limiting theexplanatory power of zonal supply security indicators. Accordingly, assessments of price resilience shouldplace greater emphasis on regional market dependencies rather than zonal generation structure.

title: Lost flexibility: Hydropower capabilities in large-scale, Pan-European Energy system models
abstract: Hydropower is an important provider of flexibility, supporting the integration of intermittent renewable energy sources. Despite the need for accurate representation of these units, large-scale energy system models face challenges when modelling hydropower due to a lack of detailed data and standardised datasets. These issues typically risk overestimating hydropower's capabilities in terms of flexibility. To address this, we analysed historical hydropower operation to develop maximum generation limits and ramping rates, as well as forced minimum generation constraints, enabling the estimation of the amount and value of lost flexibility. At the European level, the lost flexibility could amount to 140 GW/h of lost hourly ramping capability, a reduced maximum generation capacity by 68 GW, and a forced minimum generation of up to 10 GW. When applying the constraints to the North European Backbone model, a pan-European energy system model, they exposed the limitations of aggregated hydropower representations that disregard real-world operational behaviour in run-of-river and reservoir hydropower plants. The results showed that ignoring operational constraints could lead to underestimating system costs, electricity prices, and the need for other flexibility sources. Particularly areas rich in hydropower experienced significant changes in the utilisation of alternative flexibility sources, such as battery storage, pumped hydroelectric plants, and transmission volumes between bidding zones. Our study highlights the importance of better representing hydropower in large-scale, aggregated energy system models. Overall, the investigated real-world-inspired hydropower constraints are especially valuable for studies on high penetration of variable renewable energy sources, storage adoption, and development of the pan-European transmission network.​ ​

title: Dimensionality reduction framework of cathode operating conditions for PEMFC voltage behavior under high humidity: A two-index approach
A resilience-aware methodology to support data center optimal allocation considering the transmission grid’s hosting capacity
abstract: The growing demand for digital services has driven the deployment of increasingly large data centers, with individual facilities expected to reach gigawatt-scale power requirements in the near future. However, integrating such large loads into existing transmission systems requires careful planning to ensure efficient and timely grid connections while minimizing environmental impacts. In this context, this article introduces a methodology to support the optimal allocation of new data centers within an existing transmission grid. The proposed approach relies on Particle Swarm Optimization and explicitly accounts for the grid’s hosting capacity while identifying allocations that remain technically feasible under a predefined set of contingency scenarios. By jointly addressing capacity limits and operational resilience, it enables data center placements that operate within the transmission infrastructure’s limits and preserve system security under adverse conditions. A case study based on a real transmission system with high-capacity data centers already in operation is presented, and the results indicate that the methodology can provide practical decision support for both transmission system planners and data center developers.

title: A cross-level coupled analysis of a differential-pressure PEM electrolysis cell and a water electrolysis system driven by multi-objective optimisation
Degradation of polymer-electrolyte membrane fuel cells tested at 80 and 95 °C using stack hardware
abstract: To overcome heat rejection limitations, especially in transport applications, polymer-electrolyte-membrane fuel cells (PEMFCs) are required to operate at elevated temperature >80 °C. However, higher temperatures accelerate degradation of stack components. To evaluate the impact of operation temperature on durability of PEMFCs, state-of-the-art membrane-electrode-assemblies (MEAs) were investigated in single-cell configuration using stack hardware; the tests consist of 500 h operation at 80 and 95 °C including electrochemical diagnostics along with monitoring of local current-density and temperature distributions. Results showed that irreversible performance and ECSA losses are respectively 27% and 7% higher at 95 °C than at 80 °C. Reversible performance losses and the corresponding recovery of these losses are 13% and 8-11% lower at 95 °C. Current-density and temperature distributions are less homogeneous at 95 °C, and areas sustaining larger local currents and temperatures correlate with local catalyst-layer thinning. Ex-situ analyses reveal contamination of MEA by silicone due to degradation of gasket material at 95°C which deteriorates the water-management capabilities of the cell.

title: Non-iterative coordinated optimal scheduling for multi-microgrid distribution system under frequency-aware islanding constraints
Hybrid shared energy storage planning for enhanced reliability in multi-energy complementary systems: a bi-level optimization framework integrating geospatial analysis and deep learning forecasting
Data-driven perspectives on pyrolysis of heterogeneous solid waste for hydrogen production: A comprehensive review
How urban morphology shapes the potential of vehicle-integrated photovoltaics in cities across the world
Coordinated transmission-distribution load restoration under N-k contingencies: a distributed optimization and reinforcement learning approach
Rethinking spatial units in BEV fast charging planning: A meso-level mobility-based approach
abstract: Rapid battery electric vehicle adoption requires direct-current fast-charging infrastructure that is both sufficient in capacity and spatially aligned with mobility-driven demand. Conventional planning relies on administrative or grid-based spatial units that fail to capture the corridor-based nature of urban travel. This study introduces a meso-level, mobility-aware spatial framework that uses arterial road networks as the fundamental unit of analysis. BEV ownership data are redistributed from postal zones to 234 arterial zones derived from Toronto’s road network, yielding a planar adjacency graph that supports spatial smoothing and ridge-path extraction; the extracted ridges act as proxies for high-activity corridors of concentrated charging demand. A graph-based Weighted Proximity Distance metric, jointly weighted by BEV density and charger capacity, quantifies the alignment between chargers and demand corridors. The observed FLO charging network is benchmarked against 1050 randomized configurations preserving network size and capacity. A complementary equity-coverage benchmark, built around a suppressed-demand criterion, adds a fairness dimension to the same null-distribution experiment. On the demand axis, the existing network performs moderately, sitting at the 31st percentile of the null distribution and outperforming 68.9% of random placements; a further 49.5% reduction in proximity distance remains attainable. On the equity axis, however, the same network is a near-outlier, covering only 7.1% of high-equity zones against a random mean of 51.6% (bottom 0.19%), revealing a structural fairness gap that the demand-only metric does not surface. The framework offers a scalable, data-efficient foundation for demand-aware, equity-conscious DC fast charging planning.

title: Cross-sectoral carbon emission flow model based three-stage low-carbon planning framework of integrated electricity‑hydrogen-transportation system
Photo-thermal synergy and bubble dynamics in an anion exchange membrane photoelectrochemical water splitting reactor under concentrated light
Efficient dynamic-aware deep reinforcement learning for solving capacitated electric vehicle routing problems with service time windows and time-of-use electricity prices
An evolutionary planning model for hydrogen infrastructure with state transitions and endogenous hierarchy formation: A case study of the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region
First-life histories leave lasting imprints: decoding path-dependent fingerprints governing second-life battery degradation and safety
Editorial Board
Multi-objective optimisation of CCUS supply chains: Bridging economic, environmental, and safety performance
abstract: As global industries accelerate towards net-zero emissions, robust Carbon Capture, Utilisation, and Storage (CCUS) supply chains are essential for guiding strategic investments in sustainable infrastructure. This work presents a comprehensive Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) multi-objective optimisation framework for CCUS networks, integrating physical carbon management strategies with carbon pricing as a complementary mechanism. The framework simultaneously considers economic, environmental, and safety objectives by minimising total annual cost and CO 2 emissions while accounting for inherent safety risks, providing a systematic approach for evaluating scalable and sustainable CCUS configurations. A case study for Great Britain employs the augmented ϵ -constraint method to generate Pareto-optimal solutions, elucidating trade-offs among the objectives. The Pareto extremes correspond to cost-optimal designs favouring CO 2 utilisation, safety-focused solutions relying on storage and pricing, and emissions-focused designs featuring extensive CCUS, incurring higher costs and safety risks. A Nash bargaining approach then identifies a fair trade-off among objectives, reducing total cost by 28%, CO 2 emissions by 48%, and improving safety by 21% relative to extreme Pareto solutions. Comparative scenario analyses further highlight the influence of carbon pricing, enhanced CO 2 utilisation capacities, and projected electricity price reductions by 2030 on the performance of CCUS networks. Overall, the paper provides a structured framework for designing and evaluating CCUS supply chains, demonstrating how multi-objective optimisation and scenario analysis guide efficient, resilient, low-carbon infrastructure.

title: Sustainable power through fuel cells: Applications and prospects in stationary and transportation sectors
Toward trustworthy AI in real-time event-driven power system emergency control: A knowledge-surrogate-guided deep learning approach
abstract: Event-driven emergency control (EEC) is a critical stability control scheme in modern power systems to maintain secure and reliable electricity supply after large severe disturbances and support power system resilience. Higher renewable penetration increases volatility and uncertainty, necessitating emergency control systems to make faster real-time decisions in response to upcoming events. Data-driven artificial intelligence (AI) offers a promising pathway for real-time EEC using online wide-area measurements. However, owing to the statistical learning nature, existing AI-based EEC models lack the capability to provide stringent and reliable compliance with transient constraints, which undermines operational safety in security-critical setting and erodes practitioners' confidence in deploying AI for emergency control. To address this limitation, this paper proposes a novel knowledge-surrogate-guided deep learning (KSG-DL) approach that enables trustworthy real-time EEC via strong transient-constraint compliance. The KSG-DL approach is designed with the ability to effectively enforce multiple transient stability/security criteria into one EEC model, including rotor angle stability, voltage security, and frequency security. The diverse transient constraint knowledge is intelligently extracted by multiple knowledge surrogate models, which efficiently guide the main EEC model to learn optimal control strategies that satisfy these complicated constraints. Moreover, Lagrangian dual algorithm is incorporated in an adaptive training pipeline to ensure strong, balanced, and robust constraint satisfaction. Simulation studies of emergency load shedding on two power systems validate the real-time (i.e. millisecond decision-making timeframe), stringent (i.e. near 100% compliance rate), and robust (i.e. across three transient criteria) constraint compliance ability of the developed EEC model, substantially improving readiness to restore system stability and security under highly variable, intermittent operating conditions.

title: An adaptive modeling method with optimal order selection for thermostatically controlled loads
A two-stage distributed optimization for non-convex P2P energy trading in prosumer-based distribution networks
Bridging macro-trend and micro-dynamics: A robust mixed-frequency framework for mid-term load forecasting
Conflict-averse federated multi-task learning for power system stability assessment
abstract: Machine learning-based power system stability assessment has attracted significant research attention in recent years. However, most of the existing approaches treat pre-fault and post-fault assessment separately, missing opportunities to exploit their shared underlying physics and complementary insights. Besides, the learning process requires diverse training data that individual utilities cannot provide due to privacy concerns. To address these issues, a novel Federated Conflict-Averse method that unifies Stability Assessment while preserving task specialization is proposed, named (FedCA-SA). First, we reformulate federated learning (FL) as a multi-objective optimization problem where specialized clients contribute domain-specific expertise while sharing universal power system knowledge. Second, to address conflicts between different clients and tasks, we adapt conflict-averse gradient descent to the federated setting, developing a selective parameter sharing mechanism that resolves gradient conflicts between pre-fault and post-fault specialists. Third, we provide theoretical convergence analysis establishing performance guarantees for conflict-averse aggregation in task-specialized FL. Experimental validation demonstrates that our proposed FedCA-SA method achieves 96.07% accuracy for pre-fault SA while reducing false positives by 36% compared to baseline federated methods.

title: Sample-efficient LLM fault diagnosis for HVAC systems via active sampling and SHAP-guided evidence condensation
Physics-informed reinforcement learning for energy-efficient minute-scale control of split-type air-conditioning systems: Experimental validation on real hardware
A data-driven model based on parallel acceleration and BERT to improve accuracy for short-term photovoltaic power prediction
Bi-level stochastic planning and energy management of a multi-carrier energy system with electrical, cooling, heating, and hydrogen hubs
abstract: Smart multi-carrier energy systems (MCESs) have emerged as a promising solution for the coordinated operation of multiple energy carriers, enabling significant reductions in operating costs and emissions. However, their optimal planning and operation under uncertainty, particularly with the integration of hydrogen-based technologies, remain a major challenge. This paper proposes a bi-level stochastic planning and energy management framework for a smart MCES integrating electrical, heating, cooling, and hydrogen hubs. The system supplies conventional energy demands as well as fuel cell electric vehicle stations and an ammonia production plant while accounting for uncertainties in renewable energy generation, load demands, and transportation behavior. In the proposed framework, the upper level optimally designs and dispatches generation and storage units, whereas the lower level applies a demand-side response strategy based on time-of-use tariffs for electricity, heating, cooling, and ammonia production. To efficiently solve the resulting large-scale and non-linear optimization problem, an enhanced Artificial Hummingbird Algorithm (EAHA) is developed by incorporating chaotic mutation, guided evolution mutation, and quasi-oppositional-based learning (QOBL) strategies to avoid premature stagnation and enhance global search capability. Simulation results show that integrating renewable energy resources with hydrogen production using steam methane reforming reduces total cost and emissions by 35.86% and 23.39%, respectively, compared to the base case without renewable energy integration, while corresponding reductions of 22.47% and 21.91% are achieved when hydrogen is produced via water electrolysis. Furthermore, applying demand-side response reduces total operating costs by 12.15% and 10.23% for the two hydrogen production pathways, respectively. The results confirm the effectiveness of the proposed framework for achieving economically efficient and low-carbon operation of hydrogen-integrated MCESs under uncertainty.

title: A trustworthy hybrid human-LLM assisted safe reinforcement learning method for distribution network operation
abstract: Distribution network is transitioning from model-based to data-driven operations amid increasing integration of renewable energy sources, posing new challenges for operational safety and cost-effectiveness. Reinforcement learning (RL), characterized by its strong adaptability and fast response, shows significant promise in this context. However, RL suffers from poor generalization against various uncertainties and heavy labor cost due to the need for extensive model or neural network modifications and hyperparameter tuning. More importantly, once deployed, the performance of RL algorithms is highly dependent on domain expert knowledge for specific power system operation or control tasks, often relying on unrealistic assumptions of perfect knowledge acquisition. Large language models (LLMs) have achieved notable success in numerous areas and present a potential approach to replace domain expert guidance, though it raises new challenges such as hallucination and limited interpretability. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a hybrid human–LLM assisted RL framework that balances human supervision with LLM assistance to improve training generalization, efficiency and stability amid high-variance uncertainties. Furthermore, a coordination-enhanced safe multi-agent RL algorithm is introduced to improve compliance with global distribution network operating constraints under decentralized control schemes among interconnected energy assets. Case studies conducted on standard distribution test systems with a domain knowledge quantification method show that the proposed method reduces voltage violations, achieves performance within approximately 5% of the theoretical optimum under unseen scenarios, and a pilot evaluation with real human participants suggests a substantial reduction in labor costs compared to purely human-driven approaches. Overall, the proposed hybrid human–LLM assisted safe RL (HH-LLM-SRL) method offers a trustworthy solution for intelligent and safe operation of distribution networks and introduces practical labor cost as a new evaluation dimension for LLM-assisted energy system decision-making.

title: Assessing scale-dependent aeroelastic load responses of 5 MW and 22 MW wind turbines under varying atmospheric stability
abstract: The upscaling of wind turbines has extended rotor-swept areas into the atmospheric boundary layer, several hundred meters above the surface layer. Traditional wind field models have relied on neutral surface-layer characteristics. Recent research emphasizes incorporating atmospheric stability and dynamics at higher altitudes, as larger turbines experience greater load variations due to eddies comparable in size to the rotor, causing non-uniform inflow. This study evaluates a measurement-validated coherence model for aeroelastic analysis of a 5 MW and a 22 MW turbine. The model characterizes atmospheric stability using tuned coefficients and is applied alongside stability-dependent spectral wind field models. Six seeds of 30 minute simulations were conducted for each wind turbine model ranging from near cut-in to near cut-out wind speed, in intervals of 1 m/s, using on one hand, the proposed coherence model with stability-dependent spectra and on the other hand, the IEC Kaimal coherence model. Aeroelastic results reveal distinct turbine responses to atmospheric stability. The trends of higher tower fore–aft bending moments in unstable conditions and lower moments in stable conditions, together with increased blade-root flapwise moments at above-rated wind speeds under stable, high-shear conditions, are captured. Wavelet analysis confirms that larger turbines face greater load variations because eddies are smaller than the rotor, whereas smaller turbines experience more uniform frequency-time correlations with hub-height velocity. Simulations with flexible and rigid blades and towers indicate that flexibility effects are secondary to eddy size and coherence. Overall, it is demonstrated that simple stability-dependent empirical coherence and spectral models can effectively replicate the commonly observed impact of atmospheric stability on wind turbine loads.

title: Performance evaluation and transient characteristics of a kerosene-fueled SOFC-GT hybrid aviation power system for long-endurance UAVs under multi-scenario operation
abstract: Under the current aviation fuel framework, solid oxide fuel cell-gas turbine (SOFC-GT) hybrid power systems have emerged as a promising solution for long-endurance unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) owing to their high efficiency and low emissions. However, the transient performance of kerosene-fueled SOFC-GT systems over the full flight envelope remains insufficiently understood. In this study, a system level multi-scale dynamic analysis framework is developed for a kerosene-fueled SOFC-GT hybrid aviation power system. A decoupled compressor-turbine architecture with multi-loop recirculation is proposed, together with a six-loop safety constrained coordinated control strategy and a rule-based battery energy management method, to evaluate power following, thermal safety, and mission-level energy coordination under multi-scenario UAV operation. The results show that the proposed strategy enables autonomous thermal management and self-sustained steam reforming while maintaining stable power following under varying flight conditions. At 9000 m and Ma = 0.5, the system achieves a net output power of 185 kW, an efficiency of 55.63%, and a specific fuel consumption of 0.1501 kg/kWh. During the climb-to-cruise and cruise-to-descent transients, the lithium battery compensates for the temporary power mismatch induced by environmental variations and system thermal inertia. Based on the integrated mission scenario covering takeoff, climb, cruise, and descent, the battery charge/discharge demand is quantified, and a battery capacity of 33 kWh is determined. Throughout the mission, the battery SOC remains within 0.4-0.8, and the operating parameters of other system components are maintained within respective safety constraints. For a 3-ton UAV, the proposed hybrid system increases the endurance by 46.0% and reduces the total CO2 emissions by 29.7% compared with a conventional power system under a consistent comparison basis. This work provides a more realistic feasibility assessment of the application of kerosene-fueled SOFC-GT systems as UAV power sources based on transient characteristics.

title: How does AI family drive the industrial chain upgrading of solar cells?
Frequency security region of high penetration renewable energy integrated power systems: theoretical, assessment, and application

The heterogeneous charging patterns and their impacts on urban grid load across vehicle categories: An interpretable machine learning analysis
Investigation on inconsistency of cell performance for 100 kW PEM water electrolyzer stacks based on cell voltage and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy
Conditional cost–emission envelopes for decarbonizing dense urban power systems under spatial renewable scarcity and flexibility constraints
A hybrid attention-based Seq2Seq framework for EV charging load forecasting integrating meteorological factors and price elasticity
Dynamic modeling and energy optimization in aluminum electrolysis process: a systematic review of multi-physics simulation and energy consumption forecasting approaches
Stochastic planning framework for EV charging stations with distributed energy resources in unbalanced distribution networks considering ecological sustainability
Techno-economic assessment and stakeholder perspectives on agrivoltaics in East Africa
abstract: Agrivoltaics (AV) can co-produce food crops and electricity while improving water conservation in East Africa; however, a lack of understanding of stakeholder perspectives and concerns over economic viability inhibits investment and uptake of the technology. This study addresses this knowledge gap by investigating stakeholder perspectives in East Africa and quantifying the financial economics – including a breakdown of CAPEX and OPEX, net present value, return on investment, internal rate of return, payback period and levelised cost of energy – of five AV scenarios based on two case studies in Kenya and Tanzania. Both AV and conventional ground-mounted solar parks are profitable in these scenarios, with net present values ranging 765–1680 USD/kWp. Mounting structures and battery storage systems dominate the CAPEX costs, with mounting structures comprised 45% of the CAPEX without battery storage, and conventional ground-mounted systems are 16–27% cheaper to install but income from crop sales partly compensates the higher CAPEX cost of AV and facilitates profitable co-use of land. While conventional ground-mounted solar parks breakeven approximately one to three years earlier than AV in the studied scenarios, the latter can be financially competitive, offer a diversified income source from the same area of land, and concomitantly benefit the food-energy-water nexus. A feed-in tariff in Kenya would boost economic viability of both PV and AV projects. These findings indicate that AV represent a viable land-use strategy for solar energy expansion in East Africa where co-benefits from land use in addition to electricity generation are valued.

title: An efficiency driving economic analysis for hydrogen-based steel making integrated with carbon management technologies
From sector coupling to carbon neutrality: Modeling the future of energy transitions through integrated, multi-level decarbonization strategies for India
Integrating in-situ monitored membrane electrode assembly parameters with external characteristics for cross-scale durability evaluation of proton exchange membrane fuel cell
Power shortages in hydro-wind-photovoltaic complementary systems: occurring conditions, temporal patterns, and planning implications
An online fault early warning framework for wind turbines using a dynamically updated temporal fusion transformer
Identifying grid-aware representative days for fast risk-based distribution network hosting capacity analysis
Modelling, experimental validation and control of shunt pipe electrolyte rebalancing for vanadium flow batteries
abstract: A dynamic model for shunt pipe electrolyte rebalancing for vanadium flow batteries (VFBs) is developed. This work extends a physics-based, mass-conserving VFB model by incorporating a hydraulic shunt pipe between electrolyte reservoirs. The model captures the hydrostatic pressure-driven flow and redox reactions within the pipe, alongside membrane diffusion and water transport. Experimental validation on a laboratory-scale system showed excellent agreement with electrolyte-level changes in the two tanks and with several performance metrics, including charge/discharge capacity and coulombic efficiency, with a maximum relative error of 2.6%. When the shunt pipe was open, the model captured the transient flow and reaction processes in the pipe, confirming that passive hydraulic remixing effectively resolves electrolyte imbalance. The model is used to evaluate the geometry of the shunt pipe and the valve control strategies to optimise discharge capacity retention and coulombic efficiency. The analysis identifies specific pipe dimensions that allow beneficial mixing against self-discharge. Furthermore, a cycle-based periodic control method demonstrated consistent capacity retention over 125 cycles. While continuous shunt rebalancing is effective during operation, laboratory and simulation results highlight that keeping the shunt pipe open during standby exacerbates capacity loss, requiring valve closure. This confirms the model's utility as a design tool for tailoring hydraulic and control protocols in industrial VFB systems.

title: Degradation mechanism of the cathode gas diffusion layer in PEMFC stack under 2000 h heavy-duty constant-current condition: PTFE driven multi-scale synergistic effect
Two-stage fine-tuning of large language models for distribution network service restoration via CoT reasoning
Robust decisions in transactive energy systems with follower response uncertainty: A coupled pessimistic stackelberg game approach
Real-time estimation of cloud properties and surface downwelling longwave radiation from satellite imagery: A two-stage surrogate modeling approach
Lithium-ion battery state-of-health estimation for fragmented charging segments in real-world fleets
Staged transition toward net-zero in remote communities: An adaptive multi-stage stochastic-robust optimization approach
abstract: The transition of diesel-dependent communities to hybrid renewable energy systems is critical to achieving their net-zero targets, yet planning such transitions is complicated by uncertainty in technology evolution and regulatory policies such as carbon caps. This study investigates whether staged transition strategies can outperform immediate large-scale deployment by leveraging cost reductions in renewable technologies and adapting to evolving policy conditions. To this end, a multi-stage stochastic–robust optimization framework is developed that integrates adaptive robust optimization for short-term operational uncertainty with multi-stage stochastic programming to capture long-term uncertainties in technology costs and carbon constraints. The model is solved using a novel scenario-decomposable column-and-constraint generation algorithm, enabling computational tractability for large-scale applications. A 25-year case study with five decision stages and 32 scenarios demonstrates that staged transition strategies reduce annual system costs by 17.3% compared to single-stage deployment, primarily by deferring high-cost technologies and prioritizing cost-effective options such as photovoltaic-thermal and combined heat and power systems. Furthermore, explicitly modeling multiple trajectories for technology learning and carbon policies yields an additional 28.9% cost saving relative to the single-trajectory planning approach. The results also highlight the strategic role of hydrogen as a long-duration flexibility resource that enhances the integration of renewables. Overall, the study shows that the value of staged planning lies in its ability to align investment decisions with evolving technology and policy conditions, enabling more cost-effective and reliable net-zero transitions in remote energy systems.

title: Comparing MCDM methods for robust decision support in industrial energy system planning
abstract: Planning industrial energy systems requires balancing economic, environmental, and technical objectives. Multi-Criteria Decision Making (MCDM) can support this process, yet it remains unclear how strongly the chosen decision method affects the recommended system design. This study provides a systematic robustness comparison of MCDM methods for industrial energy system planning by assessing both the selected system configuration and the sizing of individual technologies under uncertain criteria weights. The analysis is based on a real industrial case study in southern Germany. About 10,000 Pareto-optimal energy system configurations were generated using a multi-objective evolutionary algorithm and a Python-based energy system model. These alternatives were evaluated with seven representative MCDM methods covering additive, multiplicative, value-based, distance-based, compromise-based, and outranking approaches. Criteria weights were derived from expert judgments using the Analytic Hierarchy Process. Robustness was assessed by perturbing the weights through Dirichlet based Monte Carlo simulation and evaluating the results using Stochastic Multicriteria Acceptability Analysis. The preferred energy systems differ only marginally across methods. All methods identify a similar technological core comprising a natural gas boiler, pellet boiler, photovoltaic system, battery storage, and thermal storage. Differences occur mainly in component sizing, especially photovoltaic and thermal storage capacities. The findings indicate that simple compensatory decision methods can provide robust and transparent recommendations. For practitioners, this means that planning efforts can focus on validating preferences, technology assumptions, and key component sizes rather than on selecting a highly complex decision method.

title: Toward trustworthy security rules for MILP-based power system operation: An uncertainty-aware extraction framework
Analytical power system transient stability assessment considering nonlinear couplings among grid following inverter-based renewable resources
abstract: The inter-inverter coupling and the complex high-order nonlinear dynamics of multiple grid-following (GFL) inverter systems present significant challenges for power system transient stability assessment. In particular, constructing a suitable Lyapunov function for such systems remains a difficult task. To address these issues, this paper develops an analytical Lyapunov function-based approach for transient stability analysis of the multi-GFL-inverter systems. The proposed Lyapunov function systematically incorporates the inter-inverter coupling effects and nonlinear damping. With the derived Lyapunov function, explicit boundaries of system’s region of attraction are estimated, and critical Lyapunov function values are established, enabling fast stability assessment. The analytical expression of the stability boundaries reveals that inter-inverter coupling tends to narrow the stability margins and a transient stability enhancement method is thereby proposed. Numerical simulations validate the proposed method and further verify the impacts of inter-inverter coupling on system transient stability.

title: Optimal scheduling of electric-vehicle fleets for vehicle-to-grid services under soft- and hard-demand-limit constraints
Impact of specific biogenic feedstocks on process design and techno-economic performance in hydrogen-enhanced biofuel production via Methanol-to-Jet
abstract: Facing climate change, all industrial sectors, including the aviation sector, must defossilize. Today, aviation heavily relies on fossil kerosene. Sustainable aviation fuels (SAF) are promising for reducing the climate impact since today’s infrastructure can be used and other alternatives, such as electrification and hydrogen, are challenging. This study examines the impact of five different raw materials (digestate, sewage sludge, pine wood, straw and beech wood) and three plant scales (100 MW, 200 MW and 500 MW of feedstock) on the techno-economic performance of SAF production process chains using entrained flow gasification for syngas generation, water electrolysis for hydrogen addition and Methanol-to-Jet as conversion technology. Hydrogen is added to the synthesis gas to enable full carbon conversion. The evaluation shows that technical performance parameters such as energy efficiencies depend only slightly on the raw material and its composition, while the effects are larger for the economics since more factors, such as gasification capital costs and feedstock prices, come into play. The results for different plant scales show that larger plants benefit significantly from economy-of-scale effects, which even outweigh the effects of feedstock choice. The production costs are 2.96-3.91 €/L, depending on scale and feedstock, where the production costs vary by up to 6% for configurations with different feedstocks and the same plant capacity. The CO 2 abatement costs are estimated to be 800–1350 €/t CO 2 . Overall, the analysis shows that both the availability of raw materials and stable operation with high full load hours are crucial for minimizing production costs.

title: Hierarchical adaptive energy management for electric tractors with hybrid energy storage systems based on operational information fusion
Two-stage distributionally robust bidding strategy of virtual power plants participating in electricity markets considering WT-PV complementarity and multiple uncertainties
State of charge estimation of real-world lithium iron phosphate battery packs combining model-based and data-driven approaches
abstract: Accurate state of charge (SOC) estimation of large-sized battery packs in real-world electric vehicles (EVs) is crucial for predicting remaining mileage and enhancing battery utilization efficiency. However, this remains challenging due to complex operating conditions and cell-to-cell inconsistencies, especially for large-sized lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery packs with a flat open-circuit voltage (OCV) plateau. Therefore, this study proposes a novel SOC estimation approach for LFP EV battery packs by combining model-based and data-driven methods. First, high-reliability labeled SOCs are obtained by combining full-charge identification, reverse ampere-hour integration (AHI), and OCV-based calibration outside plateau regions. A feature enhancement strategy with multi-deviation AHI sequence is proposed to improve feature representation capability. Then, a hybrid model incorporating convolutional neural networks and gated recurrent units (CNN-GRU) is developed to accurately estimate battery SOCs during charging processes. Finally, the estimation results at the end of charging segments are leveraged to initialize an adaptive extended Kalman filter (AEKF), which integrates a battery pack model and an online parameter identification strategy, to achieve accurate SOC estimations under complex dynamic discharging conditions. The comparison with other commonly used machine learning methods and the ablation study on CNN-GRU and AEKF are performed to highlight the superiority of the proposed method in fidelity and practicability. The results demonstrate that, with the optimal parameter combination, the proposed method achieves a root mean squared error of 1.09% based on uniform deviation distributions. More than 97% of estimates show an absolute error of less than 3% for both deviation generation methods. This work provides significant insights into state estimation and prediction of LFP battery systems for field applications.

title: LLM-guided safe reinforcement learning for energy system topology reconfiguration
abstract: The increasing penetration of renewable generation and the growing variability of electrified demand introduce substantial operational uncertainty to modern power systems. Topology reconfiguration is widely recognized as an effective and economical means to enhance grid resilience. Due to the coexistence of AC power-flow constraints and discrete switching decisions, topology reconfiguration in large-scale systems leads to a highly nonlinear and nonconvex optimization problem, making traditional methods computationally prohibitive. Consequently, several studies have explored reinforcement learning-based approaches to improve scalability and operational efficiency. However, its practical implementation is challenged by the high-dimensional combinatorial action space and the need to ensure safety during learning-based decision-making. To address these challenges, this paper presents a safe and intelligent topology control framework that integrates Large Language Models (LLMs) with a Safety Soft Actor-Critic (Safety-SAC) architecture. Operational voltage and thermal limits are reformulated into smooth safety-cost signals, enabling risk-aware policy optimization within a constrained Markov decision process. A knowledge-based Safety-LLM module is further introduced to refine unsafe or suboptimal transitions through domain knowledge and state-informed reasoning, thus guiding the learning agent toward safer and more effective switching actions. Experiments on the IEEE 36-bus and 118-bus Grid2Op benchmarks show that the proposed method consistently improves reward, survival time, and safety metrics, achieving higher reward, longer survival, and lower safety cost compared with SAC, ACE, and their safety-enhanced variants. These results demonstrate the potential of combining LLM-based reasoning with safe reinforcement learning to achieve scalable and reliable grid topology control.

title: Unpowered upward flow CO₂ refrigeration system for deep-underground cooling: thermodynamic, economic, and environmental performance
Distributed optimal power and gas dispatch using variational inequalities and cooperative games
Hyperbolic PDE-constrained decision-dependent robust planning of hydrogen energy storage systems for resilient electricity-water-gas nexus
Resilience-oriented maintenance scheduling and routing optimization for IoT-enabled offshore wind farms with forecast-informed accessibility windows and cumulative task-time uncertainty
Optimal use of high-temperature geothermal resources in a hydropower dominated electricity system
abstract: Geothermal resources support the transition away from fossil fuels and can play an important role in strengthening local energy supply and promoting social development. This paper applies a stochas tic optimization model designed to maximize expected NPV under specified constraints to estimate the optimal development of a geothermal power plant within a hydro-dominated electricity system. Electricity price series are sampled based on varying assumptions about water year variability, with probabilities assigned using historical data. Geothermal resource uncertainty is incorporated through three key stochastic factors with defined probability distributions. A case study of the geothermal f ield in Bjarnarflag in Iceland is used to illustrate the model’s application. Results show that early price spikes increase both expected profits and the optimal initial phase. This effect intensifies with a higher probability of volatile prices. In contrast, price spikes occurring late reduce expected profits and production is reduced. This response is more pronounced for larger initial phases due to higher marginal costs. Compared to fixing production levels at installed capacity, allowing moderate pro duction decreases yields a 29% higher expected NPV primarily by supporting an assertive utilization strategy. A yearly timestep and uniform well cost entails few instances where marginal well cost exceeds prices leading to production decreases. To better capture the benefit of price variations, a more detailed time step and heterogeneous well costs are necessary.​

title: Optimization configuration of hybrid energy storage in integrated energy systems
Rooftop photovoltaics and energy equity: quantifying socio-energy trade-offs in urban energy transitions
abstract: Rooftop photovoltaic systems, while central to urban decarbonization, can unintentionally exacerbate social inequalities through uneven thermal and economic outcomes. This study demonstrates that rooftop PV deployment generates inequitable socio-energy trade-offs within cities, where disadvantaged communities bear higher societal costs for the same clean-energy gains. To quantify these disparities, we developed a Socio-Energy Trade-off Index (SETI) that links PV-induced warming, heat-related health risks, and economic benefits within an integrated WRF-forced Canopy Model – Building Energy Model framework applied to six global cities. Results reveal that PV-induced warming is both widespread and unequal, with midday temperature increases from 0.27 °C in Cairo to 0.58 °C in Guangzhou and a Gini index up to 0.322. Less developed communities consistently record higher SETI values due to compact urban form and limited financing access. Furthermore, sensitivity analyses reveal that technological improvements reduce total trade-offs, with increases in panel efficiency from 17% to 25% and panel emissivity from 0.85 to 0.99 lowering SETI by up to 81.9% and 40.0–46.4%, respectively, yet these gains disproportionately benefit formal, self-financed communities, widening relative inequity. These findings reframe the Photovoltaic Heat Island (PVHI) effect as an energy-system externality, emphasizing that equitable solar deployment requires integrating efficiency and justice in urban energy transitions.

title: Assessing electrification, energy security, and equity in diverse transition contexts: a cluster-based analysis of 123 countries
Endogenizing and tracing supply-chain CO₂ emissions of power system capacity expansion: an extended input-output linear programming framework
Investigation of the seawater impact on the state-of-the-art solid oxide electrolyzes cells performance and stack components degradation
Physical-prior-regularized decoupled exogenous-aware network for trustworthy multi-energy load forecasting in commercial park-level integrated energy systems
Experimental study on flight characteristics of unmanned aerial vehicles powered by air-cooled proton exchange membrane fuel cells in high-altitude environments
Power allocation for alkaline water electrolysis clusters under current fluctuations: a model-based method for efficiency enhancement
Robust multi-objective wind farm layout optimisation under per-turbine cost uncertainty
abstract: Per-turbine construction and O&M costs are universally treated as deterministic in wind farm layout optimisation (WFLO), despite documented UK onshore LCOE uncertainty of GBP 35–62/MWh and turbine fatigue load variation of up to 25% across positions. This paper addresses that gap by proposing a multi-objective robust WFLO framework applied to the Kelmarsh Wind Farm (UK) as a wind resource and turbine characterisation data source. A Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) with BIC-optimal K = 4 component selection characterises 6 years (2016–2021) of SCADA wind climatology; Gaussian Process (GP) regression with statistical outlier removal constructs wake-corrected power curves validated across all six Senvion MM92 turbines (R 2 = 0.977–0.994). Box and Ellipsoid uncertainty sets are embedded within an NSGA-II Pareto backbone and benchmarked against classical GA and deterministic NSGA-II on identical inputs. On an 81-position design domain, the robust Box model (ε = 0.10, Γ = 2) selects 57 turbines and achieves a mean AEP improvement of 5.28% ± 0.66% over NSGA-II at identical cost (USD 3.3 × 10 7 ), confirmed statistically significant at p < 0.01 (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, 10 independent runs; W = 0) which corresponding to approximately 1.0–1.2 GWh/year additional generation and an indicative LCOE reduction of GBP 2.3/MWh against the Arup/DESNZ 2024 UK baseline. The AEP gain is non-monotone in the conservatism budget Γ, with a site-specific interior optimum at Γ = 2. The Box formulation achieves this within the same O(N·M 2 ) scalability as standard NSGA-II at only 1.3× computational overhead, offering a tractable path to deployment on large offshore wind farms.

title: Multi-fault diagnosis of second-life lithium-ion batteries for shared electric bikes using sparse cloud-based charging data and TabNet deep learning network
Linking wind-power fluctuation to degradation of PEM water electrolyzer
Predict-then-optimize: LM-MTSF provides data-driven support for distributionally robust operation optimization of active distribution networks
